narration:
The organiser taps the notices into a tidy stack, then glances at your proposed game.

“I’ll play a round. One silver apiece, stakes on the board first. Not risking my wages.”

He hasn’t agreed to twelve silver—and you have no loaded die among your established possessions, only your compass. Palming one would first require obtaining it; winning money would still depend on the game and whether the trick went unnoticed. No silver has changed hands.

The organiser rests a hand on the stack, waiting to see whether you can put up a stake. “Or were you after work?”

narration:
You leave the organiser beside his notices and take the eastbound road. Beyond the square, the buildings thin out; soon there is only the road, the fields, and the occasional cart.

Your compass keeps you on course. Food and shelter are less certain: neither provisions nor camping gear are recorded among your possessions. The journey needn’t become an ordeal, but those two days cannot simply supply themselves.
You find water at roadside troughs, but no meal comes with it. The first night passes in broken sleep beneath the overhang of an empty wayside shelter. By the second afternoon, hunger and the miles have made the walk a slow business.

Two days after leaving the square, you reach **Marrow Ford**.

The road descends between low houses to a broad, shallow river. Wheel ruts enter the water beside a line of worn marker posts; on the opposite bank, wet gravel gleams where carts have climbed out. Smoke rises from the near-bank chimneys, carrying the smell of cooking onions.

Outside a riverside cookhouse, a board reads: **HOT STEW. BOOTS OFF BEFORE ENTERING.**

You stand at the edge of the settlement, thirsty again and in need of a proper meal and rest. The road continues through the ford.

narration:
The organiser rests a thumb on the corner of the notice board.

“Then you’ll be glad the notices are already filled in.”

He gives you a moment, but doesn’t reach for a purse.

“Best-paid job I have is checking the north mill road. A carrier turned back after finding a bank washed across it. The mill needs to know whether a loaded cart can get through, and, if not, whether the old ridge track will take one. Twelve silver for a useful report: where the blockage is, how deep, what ground’s holding. Not twelve for saying you went.”

He taps a notice with a rough route sketched beneath its lettering.

“No advance to someone I don’t know. You want money for nothing, you’ll need someone with more money than sense.”

His tone stays matter-of-fact.

“I can show you the route before you decide. Can you judge ground, or is ‘hero’ the whole qualification?”

narration:
A broad-shouldered porter beside the board rolls up his sleeves. “Anyone in the square,” he repeats. “First one pinned. No punches.”

At your challenge, he steps onto a patch of bare ground and waits for you to face him. The organiser moves clear, keeping the notice board at his back.

You can take him on—but victory isn’t settled by the challenge. The porter braces as you close, trying to get both hands inside your grip.

His boast has some weight behind it. He catches your upper arm, steps across your stance, and turns with a practiced pull. Your footing goes; he follows you down rather than dropping his weight onto you.

A moment later, both your shoulders are against the dirt.

“That’s a pin,” the organiser says.

The porter immediately lets go and rises. No injury, but dust clings to your clothes, and the triumph belongs to him this time.

“Good of you to actually try,” he says, offering a hand. His grin is broad, though he doesn’t prolong the hold or demand a concession. “Most just tell me they could.”

The organiser leaves his purse where it is.

He steps back as the porter lowers his offered hand. The porter’s grin fades, but he doesn’t reach for you.

“We had a friendly bout,” he says. “Leave it friendly.”

The organiser keeps his eyes on you.

“The notices are there to be read. You don’t need a key for that. If you want work, the road assessment is still available. If you mean to take my purse, we’ve a different problem.”

Neither man advances. There’s space to step away, and the organiser hasn’t called for help—but his hand now rests protectively over the purse.

narration:
The organiser holds down a curling corner of one notice so you can read it.

“Highest total? Twelve silver, posted by **Mara Venn, the miller**. She’s got a handcart stranded on the north track—broken wheel, six sacks of flour aboard. Wants the flour brought back to her mill dry. Cart too, if it can be managed, but the twelve is for the flour.”

The notice bears a mill-wheel stamp beneath the payment terms.

“Mind, that’s twelve for the whole job, not twelve each. You’d need help or something to carry it on. She’ll lend a sound cart, but you’d have to fetch it from her.”

He taps a shorter notice beside it.

“Best pay if you’re working alone is probably this: five silver to walk the boundary markers at Bellweather pasture and report which need resetting. Posted by the tenant, **Edric Hale**. No lifting required, and he wants a report, not somebody picking a quarrel with his neighbour.”

He takes his hand off the board. “Are you after the largest purse, or the most you can earn on your own?”
